title: Anthropic's IPO Keeps Founders in Control Through a "Founder LLC" Voting Structure

Anthropic's IPO Keeps Founders in Control Through a "Founder LLC" Voting Structure

The initial public offering (IPO) queue just welcomed its most unconventional corporate creature yet. Artificial intelligence (AI) heavyweight Anthropic, the developer behind the Claude platform, officially filed its Form S-1 registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) today.

The filing sets the stage for a Nasdaq debut under the ticker ANT. But beneath Anthropic's staggering compute numbers and explosive top-line growth lies a governance framework that should stop prospective shareholders in their tracks.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Silicon Valley has long treated public investors as passive passengers. Mega-cap innovators like Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META), and Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) built modern market empires on dual- or triple-class equities. Their stock structures grant public buyers economic claims while effectively walling off boardroom power behind insider shares.

But Anthropic's proposed setup makes even those founder-friendly bastions look tame. Instead of merely weighting voting rights based on who owns the most stock, Anthropic is slicing ownership, shareholder voting, and board oversight into five distinct share classes.

The 4 Major Differences
1. A single "golden share" instead of billions of shares (Class F)

SpaceX and Meta are the same story. Musk and Zuckerberg both have total control over shareholder votes through their massive holdings of supervoting Class B shares. They have the option to convert these shares into common stock if they want to raise personal cash, but then they would gradually lose their voting power.

At Anthropic, the founders created Class F common stock consisting of a single share held by the founders' LLC. It has no economic rights (no claim to profits or dividends) but gives the co-founders 50.1% of the total vote on all general corporate matters. The vote counts of other classes don't even matter in most cases; Class F decides the outcome of simple-majority votes.

After dropping 8.3% last week, Lumentum Holdings (NASDAQ:LITE) stock is starting the last week of October trading on an auspicious note. With a financial services firm initiating coverage and taking a bullish stance on the developer of optical and photonic technologies, investors have found sufficient grounds to click the buy button.

Lumentum shares closed 8.2% higher from their closing price on Friday, Oct. 23.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Another firm sees ample room for this tech stock to run

Initiating coverage with a buy rating, StoneX set a $1,200 price target on Lumentum stock this morning. According to Thefly.com, the financial services firm based its outlook, in part, on management's acknowledgment that it has AI-related optoelectronic capacity that is effectively committed into the early part of 2029.

Based on Lumentum's closing price of $756.17 on Oct. 23, the StoneX price target implies 59% upside.

On Oct. 20, Jefferies also adopted a more bullish perspective on Lumentum stock, raising its price target to $1,250 from $1,200.

In addition to AI computing, Lumentum develops optical and photonic technologies that support the networks and infrastructure for cloud computing and other advanced communications.

Is Lumentum stock a buy now?

While StoneX sees Lumentum stock soaring in the coming months, investors would be smart to take a more cautious approach to the tech stock and not rush out to load up on shares. Lumentum stock is changing hands at 54.1 times operating cash flow, a premium to its five-year average cash flow multiple of 15.4.

For those interested in Lumentum stock, it will be important to see whether the company meets its first-quarter 2027 guidance -- revenue of $1.23 billion to $1.28 billion and adjusted diluted net income per share of $4.05 to $4.35 -- and then reevaluate whether buying shares is a smart move.

CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) stock has been battered this month as investor skepticism about the AI infrastructure trade and its steep build-out costs has grown.

After a post showing the neocloud stock's bond yields reaching as high as 15%, investors fled the stock, with some even anticipating its bankruptcy in the not-too-distant future.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Before a modest recovery on Monday in sympathy with Anthropic's IPO filing, CoreWeave stock had fallen 41% in less than three weeks, dragging down other AI infrastructure stocks with it.

However, that sell-off could be an attractive buying opportunity as CoreWeave has long been volatile, and there are a number of catalysts that could fuel its recovery. Here are three reasons why the stock could touch $100 a share by the end of the year, nearly doubling from its current price.

Image source: Getty Images.

1. Cloud capacity remains tight

The indications from AI companies that have already reported earnings this quarter, such as Space Exploration Technologies (Nasdaq: SPCX) and Meta Platforms, suggest that demand for AI compute continues to outstrip supply.

Elon Musk said that demand for SpaceX's AI infrastructure was so strong that the company anticipated a payback period of new deployments in less than a year, and that prices for older chips, like Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) H100's are even higher than they originally were due to limited supply.

Amazon (Nasdaq: AMZN) CEO Andy Jassy said that his company's cloud capacity is nearly sold out through 2027, and that a good chunk of 2028 is sold out as well. He also said the company is struggling to keep pace with demand for AI compute, which explains why Amazon and its peers are spending so much on cloud infrastructure. Amazon Web Services (AWS) is the largest cloud infrastructure provider in the world, and if Amazon is sold over the next year, that should bode well for other cloud infrastructure companies like CoreWeave.

As long as demand is outrunning supply, CoreWeave is in a strong position.

2. Its partnership with Nvidia gives it a competitive advantage

Neocloud stocks are sometimes dismissed as commodity businesses, and that's true to some extent. However, CoreWeave does differentiate itself in one important way from its peers. The company has a close partnership with Nvidia, which benefits it in multiple ways.

title: Verizon's Turnaround Is Gaining Momentum. Is This 6.5%-Yielding Dividend Stock a Buy?
detail:
Verizon's Turnaround Is Gaining Momentum. Is This 6.5%-Yielding Dividend Stock a Buy?
Matt DiLallo, The Motley Fool
Mon, October 26, 2026 at 4:20 PM EDT 5 min read
VZ
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Verizon (NYSE:VZ) is starting to look like more than just a high-yield dividend stock. The telecommunications giant added 406,000 postpaid phone customers in the third quarter, an eye-popping 820% year-over-year increase. That accelerating momentum helped drive stronger earnings and cash flow, prompting Verizon to raise its full-year outlook for the third straight quarter.

With the stock trading at less than nine times this year's expected earnings and yielding 6.5%, is Verizon stock a buy right now? Here's a look at the company's most recent quarter and its total return potential from here.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

The turnaround is gaining momentum

Verizon's third-quarter earnings rose 8.3% to $1.31 per share. That's a continuation of its strong momentum this year. It topped the 7.6% growth rate achieved in the first quarter, its best quarterly growth rate since 2021. The company delivered its strongest third-quarter postpaid phone net adds in five years and its best quarterly net account growth in over a decade. Meanwhile, its churn rate was lower year over year.

The telecom giant's ability to win high-value customers while retaining more of its existing customer base is driving expanding margins and strong cash flow. Its cash flow from operations was $11.5 billion in the quarter (up 2.2% year over year), while its free cash flow was $7.8 billion (up 12.1% year over year). Verizon has generated $18 billion in free cash flow through the first nine months of this year (a 14.3% increase), following $11.9 billion in capital expenditures. That has more than covered its dividend ($8.8 billion paid through the first nine months of this year), leaving excess cash to repurchase stock ($4 billion year-to-date) and strengthen its balance sheet.

More earnings and cash flow growth ahead

Verizon's continued improvement led the telecom giant to boost its full-year guidance for the third straight quarter. It now expects adjusted earnings-per-share growth of 7%-7.5% in 2026 (up from 6%-7%) and free cash flow growth approaching 12% (up from 9%-10% growth).

The improvement in its core wireless and broadband businesses isn't the only driver of growth. CEO Dan Schulman noted in the earnings press release that "technology leaders are choosing our fiber network to power the next generation of AI infrastructure." The company recently expanded its strategic partnership with Amazon Web Services with a landmark AI infrastructure deal valued at over $2 billion. It previously signed a deal worth more than $1 billion with Google. Meanwhile, Shulman stated on the third-quarter conference call that the company is in talks with additional companies on similar deals.

Is Verizon stock a buy?

Shares of Verizon currently trade around $43. They've fallen nearly 8% over the past month due to a post-earnings slump and a potential competitive headwind related to SpaceX. It's now trading at about 8.5 times earnings, at the midpoint of its $5.04-$5.06 per share adjusted earnings guidance range. That's quite cheap compared to the broader market, as the S&P 500 trades at around 19 times forward earnings. This low valuation is why Verizon offers such a high dividend yield.

The reason Verizon trades so cheaply is its slow growth rate. While earnings growth has accelerated this year, investors aren't yet convinced that the company can continue to grow at a mid- to high-single-digit annual rate. If it can, the company could deliver low- to mid-teens annualized total returns when accounting for its dividend income and some multiple expansion. However, if its growth rate slows again (which is very possible if SpaceX enters the U.S. mobile sector), total returns would likely be in the high single digits at best.

I think the likely outcome is somewhere in the middle. Verizon's turnaround is producing measurable results. Its valuation is modest, its dividend is well covered by free cash flow, and it could deliver roughly a 10% annualized return without requiring significant earnings growth. That's a solid outcome, especially for investors seeking income, which is why I think the stock is a buy after earnings.
